title: Grand Cru, Premier Cru
subtitle: What those words on a champagne label promise, where they came from, and what they leave for your glass to decide.

episodes.title: The Words on the Label
episodes.hook: If you have ever stood in front of a shelf of champagne and wondered whether grand cru on the label means a better wine, you are in very good company. The real answer is kinder, and more interesting, than a simple yes.
cards: Cru is a French word meaning a growth, from the verb croître, to grow. On a wine label it points to the place where the grapes grew.
So when a champagne label says grand cru or premier cru, it is telling you about where the grapes came from rather than about the house that made the wine.
In Champagne, that place is a whole village, which the French call a commune. Every vineyard within a grand cru village shares the village's rank.
This is different from Burgundy, where a grand cru is a single named vineyard, and it is that vineyard's own name you find on the label.
It differs from Bordeaux as well, where the celebrated classifications rank estates, the châteaux, rather than villages or individual vineyards.
Champagne chose the village. Seventeen villages are entitled to call their grapes grand cru, and a longer list of villages may call theirs premier cru.
The rule on the label is careful and strict. A champagne may say grand cru only if every grape in it was grown in those seventeen villages.
Premier cru follows the same principle, with one generous detail: grand cru villages may use the premier cru name too, so a premier cru blend can include their grapes.
If even a small part of the blend came from a village outside the list, the phrase has to come off the label, however lovely the wine may be.
Some labels go a step further and name the village itself, Ambonnay or Avize, for instance. Then every grape in the bottle must come from that one village.
You will not find cru classé on a champagne label. That phrase belongs to the rules of other regions, and Champagne's regulations do not permit it.
Behind grand cru and premier cru sits a ladder of percentages called the échelle des crus, which gave each of Champagne's wine-growing villages its own number.
Grand cru villages stood at the top of that ladder, at one hundred per cent, with the premier cru villages just below them, from ninety to ninety-nine.
In the final version of the scale, every other village was rated somewhere in the eighties, so the ladder had many more rungs than the two you see on labels.
The ladder itself has since been retired, yet the two phrases it gave the label are still in use, which is why you continue to see them today.
Because a rank belongs to the whole village, it is shared by every grower and every slope within it, the exceptional corners and the ordinary ones alike.
That is why some growers and writers will gently point out that some sites outside the top villages make wines every bit as fine as their grander neighbours.
Many of the great houses blend grapes from a number of villages, because blending, which the French call assemblage, is how they keep a style consistent from year to year.
A blend like that may contain superb grand cru grapes and still carry no cru at all on the label, simply because other villages have a share in it too.
So when the words are missing, please do not read it as a warning. Very often it means the winemaker chose to draw on more than one place.
And when the words are there, they are a promise about origin, kept precisely. They tell you where the champagne grew, and leave the question of how good it is to you.
episodes.setup: Why would anyone give a single number to an entire village? The answer begins far from the dinner table, with a much plainer question about what a kilo of grapes was worth.

episodes.title: A Ladder Built to Pay Growers
episodes.hook: Long before it was a phrase on a label, the échelle des crus was something far more practical: an agreement about money, settling how much a kilo of grapes from each village should fetch at harvest.
episodes.callback: Last time, we saw that grand cru on a label is a promise about the village where the grapes grew.
cards: To see why such an agreement mattered, it helps to know that champagne has long been made by two kinds of people working side by side.
On one side are the growers, the families who tend the vines. On the other are the houses, the maisons, which buy a great many grapes and blend them into wine.
Many growers have traditionally sold some or all of their harvest to the houses, so the price of a kilo of grapes has long mattered enormously in Champagne.
Every harvest raised the same delicate question: how much should grapes from one village be worth, compared with grapes from the village over the hill?
The échelle answered it with a single number for each village. That number was a percentage, and it worked in a wonderfully simple way.
Each year a price was agreed for a kilo of grapes from the top of the ladder, and every other village then received its own percentage of that price.
So a grower in a village rated one hundred received the full price, while a grower in a village rated ninety received nine-tenths of it.
The same arithmetic ran all the way down the ladder, which meant that a village's rating quietly shaped the income of every family farming there.
Because the number belonged to the village, two neighbours with very different vineyards were paid at the same rate, as long as their grapes came from the same commune.
That is where the idea we met on the label comes from. A grand cru village was, first of all, a village whose grapes commanded the full price.
The scale took shape in the early twentieth century, during years of poor harvests, fraud and anger in the vineyards that ended in rioting in 1911.
Writers date its beginning differently, and one reason is that an informal scale existed for some years before growers and houses formally agreed a common one.
From 1941, setting the price became the work of a new body that still matters greatly today, the Comité interprofessionnel du vin de Champagne.
Its name is long, so most people say the CIVC, or the Comité Champagne. Its purpose is to bring growers and houses together around one table.
Having both sides in the room mattered, because the growers wanted a fair reward for their grapes and the houses wanted a steady, affordable supply.
A shared scale also spared everyone from bargaining village by village each autumn. The arguments were about the ladder itself, and the arithmetic did the rest.
It also meant the ratings carried real weight, which helps explain why villages cared so deeply about where they stood on the ladder.
Notice what the scale never did. It did not judge any particular bottle of wine, only the grapes of a village at the moment they changed hands.
That gentle distinction is worth keeping. The ratings are best understood as part of Champagne's commercial history, rather than as a verdict on what is in your glass.
episodes.setup: A ladder agreed by people can be moved by people. Next, we watch villages climb it, and see how far its lowest rungs rose over the century.

episodes.title: How the Ladder Moved
episodes.hook: It is tempting to picture the ladder as ancient and unchanging, but it was revised throughout the twentieth century, with villages moving up its rungs and the bottom of the scale rising a long way.
episodes.callback: We have seen how the échelle turned each village's rating into a share of the price of grapes.
cards: The earliest version of the scale, drawn up in 1911, placed eleven villages at one hundred per cent, the first villages we might recognise as grand crus.
Those eleven were Ambonnay, Avize, Aÿ, Beaumont-sur-Vesle, Bouzy, Cramant, Louvois, Mailly, Sillery, Tours-sur-Marne and Verzenay.
Puisieulx, whose grapes had traditionally been harvested together with those of neighbouring Sillery, later joined them at the top, making twelve.
At the other end, the first scale reached much further down than the final one would, with some villages rated at less than half of the top price.
Over the following decades the floor was raised in stages, until no village sat below eighty per cent.
For growers on the lower rungs, each rise meant a better price for exactly the same grapes, which is why these revisions were never merely technical.
The ladder came to include the villages of the Aube, in the south, whose growers had fought hard to be counted as part of Champagne at all.
In the final scale, every Aube village sits at eighty per cent, the lowest rung, and none was ever rated higher.
That is one reason you will not find grand cru or premier cru on a bottle from the Côte des Bar, however beautiful the wine inside may be.
The best-known revision came in 1985, when five villages were promoted to grand cru together.
They were Chouilly, Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, Oger and Oiry on the Côte des Blancs, and Verzy on the Montagne de Reims.
With those five added to the twelve, the list reached the seventeen grand cru villages whose names you see on labels today.
It can be surprising to learn that Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, now one of the most admired names on the Côte des Blancs, became a grand cru only in 1985.
Promotion changed more than pride. While the scale still set prices, a village moving up to one hundred saw its growers paid the full rate from then on.
So when you meet a grand cru village today, you are seeing the latest position on a ladder that kept moving for most of a century.
It is worth holding that history lightly when you taste. A village's place reflects decisions made by people at particular moments, as well as the qualities of its slopes.
episodes.setup: Seventeen villages, then, stand at the top. Next, we find out where they are, and why they divide so largely between two grapes.

episodes.title: Seventeen Villages, Two Characters
episodes.hook: Of the seventeen grand cru villages, eleven sit on and around the Montagne de Reims and beside the Marne, most of them known for Pinot Noir, while six line the Côte des Blancs and are known for Chardonnay.
episodes.callback: We watched the ladder move until, in 1985, seventeen villages stood at the top.
cards: Champagne's vineyards are spread across several districts, yet the grand crus gather in just two of them, both close to the towns of Reims and Épernay.
The first is the Montagne de Reims, a broad wooded hill between those two towns, with vineyards wrapped around its slopes.
Nine grand crus belong to the Montagne and its edges: Ambonnay, Beaumont-sur-Vesle, Bouzy, Louvois, Mailly-Champagne, Puisieulx, Sillery, Verzenay and Verzy.
Two more sit beside the river Marne. Aÿ lies across the water from Épernay, and Tours-sur-Marne lies a little upstream, where the Montagne slopes down to the river.
For the most part these are Pinot Noir villages. Pinot Noir is a black grape, and in champagne it brings much of the structure and depth.
Bouzy and Ambonnay, on the Montagne's southern side, are among the names most often spoken of when people talk about grand cru Pinot Noir.
Verzenay and Mailly-Champagne lie on the northern side of the hill, a reminder that the ratings were never simply a reward for facing the sun.
Not every Montagne grand cru is so single-minded. Sillery and Puisieulx grow a good deal of Chardonnay and Meunier alongside their Pinot Noir.
The second district is the Côte des Blancs, a long slope facing east and running south from Épernay, and its name tells you what to expect.
Blancs means whites, and here the white grape Chardonnay is grown almost to the exclusion of everything else.
Its six grand crus are Chouilly, Oiry, Cramant, Avize, Oger and Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, which you meet in roughly that order as you travel south.
Their wines are often described as precise, fresh and long-lived, though every producer interprets these villages in their own way.
Beneath all of these villages lies chalk, the soft white rock that underpins Champagne's finest slopes and gives the region so much of its character.
Because one rank covers two districts and two grapes, two grand cru champagnes can be quite different in character while carrying exactly the same words.
A blanc de blancs, made only from white grapes, is the natural home of Côte des Blancs Chardonnay, and its label may name a single village.
A blanc de noirs, made only from black grapes, often draws on the Montagne and Aÿ, though black grapes are grown in a great many other villages too.
Many celebrated blends join Pinot Noir from the Montagne with Chardonnay from the Côte, a classic example of assemblage, the art of blending, across villages.
You may wonder about Meunier, Champagne's third great grape. It is grown very widely, yet it is not the main grape of any of the seventeen grand cru villages.
That says more about where Meunier grows than about its quality. Its heartland is the Vallée de la Marne, where the ladder placed many villages lower down.
episodes.setup: The seventeen are only the very top. Next, we step down a rung, to premier cru and the many villages that stood between the summit and the floor.

episodes.title: Premier Cru and the Villages in Between
episodes.hook: Premier cru is often read as second best, but it is really a wide band of villages, each once with its own number, lying between the very top of the ladder and the many villages below.
episodes.callback: We found the seventeen grand crus divided between the Montagne de Reims, the Marne and the Côte des Blancs.
cards: On the final scale, premier cru villages were rated between ninety and ninety-nine per cent, so the band held ten possible steps.
Today there are forty-two premier cru villages, the figure given by France's consumer authorities in their 2022 guidance on reading champagne labels.
You may meet other counts in books and online, from forty-one to forty-four. We use forty-two because it comes from an official source.
Among the villages at the top of the band, at ninety-nine, just one step below grand cru, were Mareuil-sur-Aÿ and Tauxières-Mutry.
Mareuil-sur-Aÿ lies right beside the grand cru of Aÿ along the Marne, which shows how a single step could separate close neighbours.
Further down, villages such as Vertus at ninety-five, and Hautvillers and Cumières at ninety-three, show how varied the band was.
Vertus is the southern neighbour of Le Mesnil-sur-Oger on the Côte des Blancs, which again places a premier cru right beside a grand cru.
Premier cru villages are found on the Montagne de Reims, in the Marne valley and on the Côte des Blancs, often in the same landscapes as the grand crus.
The rule on the label mirrors grand cru: premier cru may appear only if every grape comes from premier cru or grand cru villages.
Because the band was so wide, while the scale set prices, a premier cru blend could hold grapes priced at anything from ninety to one hundred per cent of the top rate.
Below premier cru came every other village, which French writers call autres crus, meaning simply other crus.
On the final scale they ranged from eighty to eighty-nine per cent, and there were far more of them than grand and premier crus put together.
Many lie in the Vallée de la Marne, where Meunier is widely grown, and further south in the Côte des Bar, in the Aube.
Damery, in the Marne valley, stood at eighty-nine, a single step short of premier cru, a reminder of just how fine the line could be.
Autres crus carry no special words on the label, yet many fine champagnes are made from their grapes, whether on their own or in blends.
In recent decades a number of growers in these villages have built fine reputations of their own, bottling wines that carry their village's name with pride.
So the middle and lower rungs deserve a curious eye rather than a cautious one, because a rank tells you about price history, not about the person who made the wine.
episodes.setup: For most of the century, the ladder decided what grapes were worth. Next, we see how that role came to an end, and why the words survived it.

episodes.title: The Ladder Comes Down
episodes.hook: The échelle did not end on a single day. Its hold on grape prices loosened in stages from 1990, and the scale itself was formally retired in 2010, while grand cru and premier cru lived on.
episodes.callback: We explored the wide band of premier cru villages and the many autres crus below them.
cards: For decades the price of grapes was set each year within the CIVC, the body created in 1941 to bring growers and houses together.
Each village's rating then turned that price into a figure for its own grapes, exactly as the arithmetic of the ladder intended.
In 1990 that arrangement changed. After growers and houses failed to agree a new interprofessional contract, the binding price gave way to an indicative one.
European competition rules, which take a dim view of prices fixed across a whole industry, were part of the pressure behind that change.
An indicative price is a guide rather than a rule. Growers and houses could now agree their own terms, and the old percentages remained a natural point of reference.
Over the years that followed the remaining guidance fell away. Sources differ on exactly when prices became fully free, placing it between about 2000 and 2004.
Today houses and growers negotiate directly, through contracts of their own, and the Comité Champagne no longer sets a price for grapes.
The Comité does still help manage the size of each harvest, which in turn affects how many grapes there are to buy.
With pricing gone, the scale had lost its original purpose. It was formally retired in 2010, the year a new decree set out the rules of the Champagne appellation.
What survived were the two phrases. The appellation's rules keep a list of grand cru villages and a list of premier cru villages, along with the labelling rules we met earlier.
So the seventeen and the forty-two are now fixed lists of names rather than percentages, and no village moves up or down through a negotiation over price.
That is how you can still find grand cru and premier cru on bottles today, even though the system that created them no longer exists.
The old percentages have not been forgotten, though. Growers, merchants and writers still quote them, and they still colour how villages are spoken of.
Grapes from the most celebrated villages still tend to fetch higher prices, which shows how long a reputation can outlast the rule that helped to form it.
There has been talk of reforming the classification, perhaps by rating individual vineyards rather than whole villages, but the 2024 version of the rules still lists villages.
For a reader, the lesson is a calm one. The words on the label are a living part of the rules, while the percentages behind them now belong to history.
episodes.setup: The ladder was born in a turbulent year. Next, we go back to 1911, when the anger of Champagne's growers spilled into its streets and cellars.

episodes.title: The Year the Vineyards Rioted
episodes.hook: In 1911 Champagne's growers rioted, wrecking cellars and pouring wine into the Marne. The ladder was first drawn up that same year, and to understand it, it helps to understand the anger, and the boundary at its heart.
episodes.callback: We followed the ladder to its retirement in 2010 and saw the words on the label survive it.
cards: To understand 1911, we need to go back a few years, to a time when Champagne's growers were already under great strain.
A run of difficult harvests had been hit by mildew, frost and phylloxera, an insect that kills vines by attacking their roots, and the 1910 harvest was a disaster.
At the same time, some houses were buying cheaper grapes and wine from outside the region, which growers felt undercut them and damaged the name of champagne.
In 1908 the government had drawn the first official boundary of the Champagne area, taking in vineyards of the Marne and the Aisne but leaving out the Aube.
Growers in the Marne hoped the boundary would protect them from grapes brought in from elsewhere, while in the Aube, being left outside felt like a deep injustice.
The Aube's growers had long sold grapes to Champagne's houses, so they could not see why they should suddenly be treated as outsiders.
In January 1911 anger turned into action. In Damery and Hautvillers, growers intercepted loads of grapes and wine brought in from outside and tipped them into the Marne.
Early in 1911 the Aube's exclusion was confirmed, and thousands of its growers gathered in protest, including a very large demonstration in Troyes.
Now the two sides wanted opposite things. The Aube wanted to be let in, and the Marne was determined to keep the boundary where it was.
In April, a move in the French Senate seemed to the Marne's growers to put the boundary in doubt, and the most serious rioting began.
Aÿ, the grand cru village beside the Marne, suffered worst. Cellars were broken into and set alight, and bottles and barrels of wine were destroyed.
The government sent large numbers of soldiers to restore order, though accounts of exactly how many differ widely.
In June 1911 a compromise was decreed. The Aube was admitted as a second zone, allowed to make champagne, but in a separate and lesser category.
It was an uneasy settlement, and the question was only fully resolved in 1927, when the second zone was abolished and the Aube came fully inside the boundary.
In that same turbulent year of 1911, the first version of the échelle des crus was drawn up, placing every village it covered on a ladder of grape prices.
You may hear it said that the Aube rioted because its villages were rated so low on the ladder. The fuller story is a little different.
In 1911 the Aube's struggle was over whether it belonged inside the Champagne boundary at all, and that question, rather than a percentage, brought its growers onto the streets.
It is easy to see how the two stories became tangled, because the Aube did end up on the lowest rung, where every one of its villages sits at eighty per cent.
The riots are remembered as a turning point, and they are often described as one of the pressures behind France's later system of protected appellations.
So when you see grand cru on a label, you are looking at the calm end of a story that began, in part, with wrecked cellars and wine poured into a river.
episodes.setup: We have followed the ladder from the riots to its retirement. Finally, we gather what held up, what changed, and what we chose to leave out.

episodes.title: Scorecard
episodes.hook: Every thread here ends with an honest account. This is where we gather what has held up, what has been overtaken by events, and what we chose to leave out, with our reasons, so that you can trust the rest.
episodes.callback: We went back to 1911, when riots in the Marne and protests in the Aube surrounded the birth of the first ladder.
cards: First, what has held. Grand cru and premier cru on a champagne label still describe where the grapes grew, and they promise nothing beyond that.
The ranks still belong to whole villages rather than to individual vineyards, which remains the clearest difference from Burgundy.
There are still seventeen grand cru villages, the seventeen reached in the 1985 revision, and their names are written into the appellation's rules today.
Grand cru villages may still use the premier cru name as well, so a premier cru blend may include grand cru grapes.
Next, what has been overtaken. The percentages no longer set any price. That role began to fall away in 1990, and the scale was formally retired in 2010.
The bands we described, one hundred for grand cru, ninety to ninety-nine for premier cru and eighty to eighty-nine for the rest, belong to the final version of the scale.
Earlier versions looked quite different, with fewer villages at the top and a much lower floor, which is one reason older sources can seem to disagree.
Grape prices are now negotiated freely, though the old reputations are still reflected in what grapes from the most famous villages tend to cost.
Some popular versions deserve a gentle correction. Grand cru does not promise a better wine, only a particular origin, and fine champagne comes from every rung.
The Aube did not riot in 1911 over a low rating. Its growers were fighting to be included within the Champagne boundary, which was finally settled in 1927.
And the scale did not vanish suddenly in 2010. Its pricing role had ended years before, and 2010 closed the chapter formally.
Finally, what we left out, and why. We have not given a single founding year, because the scale was drawn up informally in 1911 and formally agreed some years later.
We gave forty-two as the number of premier cru villages because it comes from an official source. Other books give figures from forty-one to forty-four.
Some villages are said to have held different ratings for different grapes. Our sources disagreed about which villages and which grapes, so we have not repeated it.
We have not said what share of Champagne's vineyards lies in grand cru or premier cru villages, because the figures we found conflicted too widely to trust.
We also left out the dramatic numbers that often accompany the riots, such as how many soldiers were sent, because the accounts differ so greatly.
And we have not ranked one grand cru above another. That question belongs to your own glass, and to the growers and houses who know each village best.
Thank you for reading this far. We hope the words on the next label you pick up feel a little more like old friends.
